      Which neighbourhoods of hashtag#Narmadapuram are most vulnerable to urban flooding?
      Floods are not just the result of heavy rainfall. They are shaped by a combination of terrain, land use, and where people live. Understanding these factors before the monsoon is essential for building more resilient cities.

      At the Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, under the guidance of Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal, our team carried out a data-driven flood risk assessment for Narmadapuram using 44 years of rainfall records together with terrain, land cover, and population datasets, all derived from publicly available sources. No field surveys. No proprietary data. Just an open and transparent methodology that can be replicated anywhere.

      The assessment covered all #33 municipal wards, integrating flood likelihood, terrain vulnerability, and population exposure. Instead of averaging these indicators, the methodology highlights wards where all three factors coincide, providing a more realistic picture of urban flood risk.
      The analysis identifies Ward 2 (Shivaji Ward), Ward 3 (Jayprakash Ward), Ward 4 (Lal Bahadur Shastri Ward), Ward 5 (Jawahar Ganj Ward), Ward 6 (Indira Ward), and Ward 30 (Narmada Ward) as the Very High Flood Risk wards. The High Flood Risk category includes Ward 1 (Shastri Ward), Ward 15 (Malakhedi North Ward), Ward 29 (Golpur Ward), and Ward 31 (Govindpura Ward).
      These insights can support municipal authorities in prioritizing drainage upgrades, emergency preparedness, and climate-resilient infrastructure investments. More importantly, they demonstrate how open data can be transformed into practical information for urban planning and disaster risk reduction.

      As climate variability increases, shifting from reactive flood response to proactive flood preparedness will be key to making our cities safer and more resilient.

      RESEARCH ALERT!

      Numerical weather models routinely miss atmospheric river landfall by hundreds of kilometers, even days out — the physics is just too hard to model directly. This paper in Atmospheric Research skips the physics altogether, training a deep learning model to learn AR behavior straight from 8 years of global reanalysis data and forecast where one will move next.

      Title: An Innovative Approach to Predict Atmospheric Rivers: Exploring Convolutional Autoencoder

      Authors: Shivam Singh, Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal
      Journal: Atmospheric Research · Apr 2023
      🔗 Read the paper: https://lnkd.in/dyRDMGBi


      Key Highlights:

      - Trained on 128,521 AR objects detected across 8 years of global ERA5 data (2011–2018).
      - Learns from 10 consecutive 6-hourly AR snapshots to predict the next one genuine forecasting, not just detection.
      - Scored SSIM 0.739 / PSNR 64.42 on unseen test data roughly 4× better than a comparable Conv LSTM benchmark from prior work.
      - One of the first fully data-driven models built to forecast future AR states rather than just detect current ones.

      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, DST - Centre for Policy Research, IIT Indore

      Research Alert!

      Most Himalayan hazard studies pick one valley, one event type, one disaster and stop there. This study in Earth's Future (Wiley, AGU) asks a bigger question: what happens when you model where every rockfall, ice avalanche, and landslide across the entire Hindu Kush Karakoram Himalaya could travel and then check what's actually standing in the way? Tracing mass movement trajectories across six mountain ranges spanning eight countries, the work delivers one of the first regional-scale hazard and exposure assessments ever produced for the world's highest terrain.

      Title: Mass Movement Hazard and Exposure in the Himalaya
      Authors: Saket Dubey, Ashim Sattar, Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal, Simon Allen, Holger Frey, Umesh K. Haritashya, Christian Huggel
      🔗 Read the paper: https://lnkd.in/d4cNFCUz


      Key Highlights:
      - Six mountain ranges modeled end-to-end (Hindu Kush, Karakoram, Western, Central & Eastern Himalaya, Hengduan Shan) the first trajectory-based hazard model built for the whole HKKH.
      -1,339 fatal landslide events (2007–2016) match the modeled hazard zones almost exactly 41% of them in Central Himalaya alone.
      - 3.6 million buildings, 0.2 million km of waterways, and 0.5 million km of roads screened for exposure one of the largest infrastructure sweeps ever done for the Himalayas.
      - Karakoram has the highest mass movement density and the highest exposure of buildings and roads, despite having just 3.3% of Central Himalaya's building density.
      - Central Himalaya has the most exposed rivers and today's highest population exposure, out of 110.8 million people living across the HKKH.
      - 103.3 million people is the swing in exposed 2100 population between the best (SSP1) and worst (SSP3) case scenarios.
      - 70% of 3,601 existing glacial lakes already sit in a mass-movement path. Eastern Himalaya is the GLOF hotspot today, but 832 new Karakoram lakes could flip that in the future.

      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Divecha Centre for Climate Change, IISc, University of Zurich, University of Dayton, American Geophysical Union

      Research Alert!
      Conventional glacier studies count lakes and stop there but a lake's size isn't what makes it deadly. This study in Water Resources Research (Wiley, AGU) asks the question that matters for Himalayan disaster planning: which of India's glacial lakes are actually primed to burst, what sits downstream in the flood path, and does the biggest lake even pose the biggest threat? Mapping 329 glacial lakes across five Himalayan states from satellite imagery, the work delivers one of the highest-resolution GLOF hazard and risk assessments ever produced for the Indian Himalayas.

      Title: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Hazard, Downstream Impact, and Risk Over the Indian Himalayas

      Authors: Saket Dubey and Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal
       Discipline of Civil Engineering, IIT Indore
      🔗 Read the paper: https://lnkd.in/dmz9NdzP


      Key Highlights:
      329 glacial lakes (>0.05 km²) delineated from Sentinel-2 & Landsat-5 imagery one of the most detailed GLOF inventories built for India to date.

      Hazard modeled from six drivers (avalanche, rockfall, upstream GLOF, moraine stability, ice cores, lake expansion) and combined with downstream exposure to rank every lake.

      23 lakes classified very high risk, 50 high risk Sikkim alone accounts for 17 of the 23 very-high-risk lakes, more than any other state or union territory.
      67 lakes threaten at least one hydropower system, a direct hit on infrastructure given that 68% of Himalayan hydropower plants sit on potential GLOF tracks.

      The twist: Gurudongmar Lake carries the single largest potential flood volume (49.89 × 10⁶ m³), yet Shakho Cho and Khangchung Tso rank as the most dangerous overall proof that flood volume alone doesn't predict risk.
      Lake area grew 15.84% between 1993-2018, but only one lake in the entire study (South Lhonak, Sikkim) has ever had a mitigation attempt.

      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, American Geophysical Union, Wiley

      After a Flood, the River May Not Be the Same: A Summer River-Safety Reminder

      As the summer aquatic recreation season begins, many people are returning to rivers, lakes, and streams for swimming, tubing, kayaking, and other activities. One important reminder: clear water does not always mean safe water — and a familiar river may not behave the same way after a major flood.

      I recently prepared a brief in response to an inquiry about whether the Guadalupe River in the Texas Hill Country was safe for swimming nearly one year after the deadly July 2025 flood. The specific case is the Guadalupe River, but the broader lesson applies to many flood-affected rivers elsewhere.

      Post-flood recreation safety is not only about bacteria or visible debris. Current E. coli testing, recent rainfall and flow conditions, water clarity, submerged debris, unstable banks, damaged access points, altered currents, scour holes, and other post-flood channel changes all matter.

      A major flood can reshape the riverbed, undercut banks, move logs and rocks, damage boat ramps, create new drop-offs or scour holes, and leave hidden hazards beneath the surface. Even when water-quality results have returned to normal, the physical river environment may still have changed.

      The infographic below highlights the key points.

      The full brief is available at the following web link:
      https://lnkd.in/gsQ2hAh4


      A companion video is also available here:
      https://lnkd.in/gNkAc7PK


      My key message is simple:

      After a major flood, do not assume a river is safe simply because the water looks clear or because time has passed. Check current water-quality advisories, recent rainfall and flow conditions, access-point safety, and possible post-flood channel hazards before returning to the water.

      Wishing everyone a safe and enjoyable summer recreation season.

      🌊 Upper Narmada Basin Water Quality Assessment Report (2016–2025) 📊
      A comprehensive assessment of water quality in the Upper Narmada Basin has been carried out using 9 years (2016–2025, April–March) of monitoring data collected from 24 monitoring stations.
      The report presents a detailed analysis of Physical, Chemical, and Biological water quality parameters to evaluate the spatial and temporal status of the river system and support sustainable water resource management.
      Report Highlights:
      ✅ 24 monitoring stations across the Upper Narmada Basin
      ✅ 9 years of continuous water quality data (2016–2025)
      ✅ Analysis of Physical, Chemical, and Biological parameters
      ✅ Long-term trends and station-wise assessment of water quality
      The analysis is based on water-quality monitoring data from the Madhya Pradesh Pollution Control Board (MPPCB). Their long-term monitoring efforts have been instrumental in understanding the health of the Upper Narmada Basin.

      Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)

      According to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the permissible limit for Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) in surface water is 3 mg/L or less.
      The results indicate that the average BOD values at all sampling stations remained well within the BIS permissible limit, ranging from 0.95 mg/L to 1.99 mg/L, suggesting generally good water quality with respect to biodegradable organic pollution.
      📖 For detailed findings, visualizations, and the complete report, visit
      Website: https://cnarmada.org/

      Narmada River Basin: Night Lights, Economic Insights( Demographic Report September 2024)
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      The Demography of Narmada River Basin Report by cNarmada uses satellite-derived night light intensity as a proxy for economic activity along with GDP data.
      Here's what the light tells us 👇
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      🌑 Upper Basin
      The upper basin's forested, sparsely settled regions remains comparatively less luminous in 2012, reflecting low economic density across most of the region. The clear exception is Jabalpur city, which stands out as the most luminous zone in the entire upper basin.

      🌑 Middle Basin
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      The most visible transformation across the decade. By 2021, the Middle Basin shows a marked expansion of mid-intensity light clusters across agricultural and peri-urban zones, pointing to growth in trade, small industry, and rural market activity.

      🌑 Lower Basin
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      Bharuch and surrounding industrial districts already showed concentrated brightness in 2012. By 2021, that intensity deepens and spreads, consistent with the area's growing industrial and port-linked economic activity near the river mouth.

      📘 Research from our lab: Aerosol Atmospheric Rivers
      Air quality is studied as a local problem. Increasingly, the evidence says it is not.
      This is the focus of our book from the Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore :

      📘 "Aerosol Atmospheric Rivers: Availability, Spatiotemporal Characterisation, Predictability, and Impacts" Published by Springer in the SpringerBriefs in Applied Sciences and Technology series.

      Authored by Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal and Dr. Kuldeep Singh Rautela, the book examines how concentrated aerosol pathways move particulate matter across regions and what that means for air quality, climate, and public health.

      Inside the book: -
      -Detection and characterization of Aerosol Atmospheric Rivers
      -Data Mining & AI/ML applied to aerosol pollution analysis
      -Risk assessment linked to particulate matter concentrations
      -Science-backed mitigation, adaptation, and resilience strategies

      Narmada River Basin: The Tribal Hotspots That Sustains the River (September 2024)
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      A critical yet often overlooked dimension of the Narmada Basin's demography is its tribal composition. The significance presence of Scheduled Tribes in many districts makes the basin unique in terms of social composition.

      Here's what the report on Demograpy reveals 👇
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      🌿 Upper Basin — Mandla, Dindori, Betul, and Chhindwara are home to large indigenous groups, deeply connected to the basin's dense forests and river tributaries.

      🌿 Middle Basin — Districts like Dhar, Barwani, Khargone, and Alirajpur carry some of the highest concentrations of tribal communities in all of Madhya Pradesh.

      🌿 Lower Basin — In Gujarat, tribal communities form the significance presence in several districts. The river here flows through lands that indigenous people have stewarded for generations.
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      These communities have historically been among the most effective custodians of forest and river ecosystems.

      Pleased to share a major milestone from our Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore
      We have been granted an Indian Patent in the domain of Wetland Science and Remote Sensing Technology!
      Congratulations to Dr. Vijay Jain , Utkarsh Yadav, and Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal
      Patent: Method and System for Risk Assessment and Management for a Wetland
       (Patent No. 589337 | Granted 14 May 2026)

      This invention presents a data-driven framework integrating climate, hydrological, and environmental datasets to assess wetland risk in real time. It evaluates hazards from both climate change-induced precipitation extremes and anthropogenic pressures, computes vulnerability through Wetland Health and Exposure Scores, and generates automated conservation and mitigation reports enabling informed decision-making for wetland restoration.

      Narmada River Basin: Demographic Story (September 2024)

      The Narmada Basin spanning Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharshtra and Gujarat 20.8 million people across the basin. But the distribution is far from uniform.

      Here's what the data tells us 👇
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      🔷 Upper Narmada Basin
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      🔴 High population districts:
      - Jabalpur — 2,425,715 (dominant urban hub)
      - Narsimhapur — 1,077,182
      - Mandla — 914,427
      - Hoshangabad — 703,092

      🟡 Low population districts:
      - Umaria — only 6,748
      - Sehore (basin portion) — 60,939
      - Sagar (basin portion) — 48,714
      - Rajnandgaon — 23,081
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━


      🔷 Middle Narmada Basin
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      - Khargone — 1,834,133 (most populous district of the Middle Narmada Basin)
      - Dhar — 1,440,006
      - Khandwa — 1,282,756
      - Barwani — 1,103,143
      - Bhopal (small part of bhopal district) — only 1,457 people

      🔷 Lower Narmada Basin
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      - Vadodara — 11.7 lakh (largest population in Lower Basin)
      - Bharuch — 9.0 lakh (highest density: 550 persons/sq km)
      - Narmada district — 4.8 lakh
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      Understanding this population gradient, from dense agrarian MP to industrialised Gujarat coast, is essential for targeted river basin governance.

      Narmada River Basin: Reading the Population Density Story (September 2024)

      The latest Demography of Narmada River Basin Report by cNarmada, IIT Indore & IIT Gandhinagar for NRCD/Ministry of Jal Shakti maps how population pressure is distributed across the basin's three sub-basins.
      Here's what the district-level density data reveals 👇

      ▶ Upper Basin -
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

      Umaria (582) and Jabalpur (519) are the most densely populated districts Jabalpur being the dominant urban centre of the upper basin.
      Tribal and forested districts like Dindori (128), Mandla (136), and Chhindwara (91) remain sparsely settled.

      ▶ Middle Basin -
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

      Jhabua (525) and Bhopal (465) stand out as high-pressure nodes.
      Core basin districts, Dhar (291), Barwani (282), Dhule (276), show substantial density, reflecting agrarian and tribal population concentrations.
      Hoshangabad (105) and Sehore (partial area, 19) represent low-density transitional zones.

      ▶ Lower Basin -
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

      Bharuch (550) leads the lower basin, driven by industrial urbanisation near the river mouth.
      Panch Mahals (334), Chhota Udepur (300), and Vadodara (300) show moderate-to-high densities.
      Alirajpur (196) connects the MP and Gujarat portions at relatively lower pressure.
      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

      The pattern is clear: urban cores and agricultural lowlands carry disproportionate demographic loads, while tribal and forested areas remain ecologically buffered for now.

      Understanding where people live along the river is the first step toward planning water resource management, sanitation infrastructure, and climate adaptation strategies that actually reflect ground reality.

      📘 Read the full report: https://lnkd.in/g4TWEgyi


       🌐 Website: https://cnarmada.org/

      Celebrating the 12th International Yoga Day on the banks of the sacred Narmada
      On 21 June 2026, members of cNarmada joined citizens, officials, and community leaders at the historic Ahilya Fort and Narmada Ghat in Maheshwar, Madhya Pradesh, to mark International Yoga Day. The event was organized by the District Administration, Khargone, and brought together nearly 500 participants for a morning yoga session conducted under the Common Yoga Protocol of the Ministry of AYUSH.

      For us, this was more than a wellness gathering. Practising yoga along the flowing waters of the Narmada was a reminder of the deep connection between human well-being and the health of the river systems we depend on. Our participation, guided by Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal and Prof. Pritee Sharma, allowed us to engage directly with local communities and stakeholders and to share the goals of the cNarmada initiative sustainable river basin management, environmental conservation, and the long-term preservation of the Narmada ecosystem.

      We believe that protecting the Narmada is inseparable from the well-being of the people who live alongside it. Events like these help build the public awareness and community partnerships that meaningful river research and conservation require.

      Pleased to share the announcement! Thanks Dr Andre Lindner and Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal Swati Sharma for your leadership! We look forward to horizontal and vertical expansion to global impacts by knowledge integration on climate action, sustainability, green transformation, health and disaster resilience towards holistic and common future’s resilience. Experts and authors worldwide are encouraged to submit their proposals.
      Andre Lindner • 3rd+ Managing Director and Advisor Internationalization of the School of Civil and Environmental Engineering at TUD | Dresden University of Technology 2mo •
      The climate crisis is no longer a “future risk.” It is the operating condition of our century.

      Floods, fires, heatwaves, droughts, supply-chain disruptions, urban vulnerability, fragile infrastructures, biodiversity loss, public health emergencies - these are not isolated events. They are signals from a planet whose systems are under pressure.

      In the spirit of World Environment Day 2026 (      hashtag#NowForCllimate), I would like to invite contributions to the Springer Nature book series "Disaster Resilience and Green Growth", for which I serve as one of the Series Editors.

      This series is for work that does more than describe the crisis. It is for books that ask: How do we build cities that can absorb shocks rather than collapse under them? How can green growth become more than a slogan? What can nature-based solutions teach engineers, planners, economists, and policymakers? How do we move from disaster response to anticipatory governance? What does resilience mean when climate extremes become the new baseline?

      We are looking for ambitious monographs and edited volumes that connect disciplines, regions, methods, and practices - especially work at the intersection of:

      🌍 climate adaptation and mitigation
      🌱 green growth and circular economy
      🏙 resilient cities and sustainable infrastructure
      ⚠️ disaster risk reduction and emergency governance
      🌿 ecosystem resilience and nature-based solutions
      🤝 policy, justice, public health, and sustainable development

      The world does not need another shelf of books that merely document what is going wrong. It needs rigorous, imaginative, usable knowledge about what can still be built, repaired, redesigned, governed, protected, and transformed. That is the ambition of this series.

      More information and submission details:
      https://lnkd.in/dtQZuWZ7


      I would be very glad to hear from researchers, practitioners, and interdisciplinary teams working on bold book ideas in this space.

      New Research Alert!
      Air pollution causes approx 7 million premature deaths every year, yet our ability to monitor and forecast its most extreme events still lags behind. This review in Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews asks a question that matters for public health and policy: how do we reliably measure, model, and predict extreme air pollution before it becomes a crisis?

      The work delivers a 20-year synthesis (2005 to 2025) of monitoring technologies and modeling approaches, showing that no single method works alone and that integration is the way forward.

      Title: A review of extreme air pollution measurement and modeling techniques with applications

      Authors: Dr. Kuldeep Singh Rautela, Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal IIT Indore and Prof. Manju Mohan IIT Delhi

      🔗 Read the paper: https://lnkd.in/ggN_rf28


      Key Highlights:
      - Synthesizes the full toolkit: ground networks, satellites, low-cost IoT sensors, and deterministic, ML, and hybrid models.
      - No single method wins. Hybrid frameworks that fuse physics-based and data-driven models perform best for extreme events.
      - ML calibration transforms low-cost sensors, lifting accuracy (R²) from about 0.40 to 0.99.
      - Data assimilation cuts PM2.5 prediction bias by up to 91.8%.
      - Case studies: Delhi hit 300 to 400 µg/m³ in peak events, Beijing 250 to 300 µg/m³, with regional transport driving 32 to 63% of Beijing's pollution.
      - The path forward: multi-platform data fusion, explainable AI, and uncertainty-aware forecasting for real-time early warning.

      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi

      Research from our lab: AI Innovation for Water Policy and Sustainability

      Water management is often treated as an engineering problem. Increasingly, the evidence says it is also a policy and intelligence problem.
      This is the focus of our book from the Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore:

      📘 "AI Innovation for Water Policy and Sustainability"
      Published by Springer in the Springer Briefs in Water Science and Technology series.

      Authored by Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal, Dr. Sachidanand Kumar , and Dr. Akhilesh Gupta (Department of Science and Technology, Government of India), the book examines how artificial intelligence can reshape the way we manage, conserve, and govern water resources in an era of rising demand and growing scarcity.

      Inside the book:
      - Basics of AI for water management
      - AI-driven approaches to water conservation
      - AI applications in water treatment
      - AI for evidence-based water policy
      - A framework for the future of AI in water

      Available now: https://lnkd.in/dXsgwMND

      Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal reposted this
      Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore 2,853 followers 2mo •
      New Research Alert!
      As climate change reshapes the hydrology of the world's most fragile ecosystems, this study in Physics and Chemistry of the Earth (Elsevier) tackles a question that conservation planners can no longer afford to get wrong: when flood risk and rainfall extremes don't line up, where should limited protection resources actually go?
      The work shows that the wettest sites are not always the riskiest ones, and proposes an integrated framework that fuses non-stationary extreme-value statistics, fuzzy-logic risk assessment, and CMIP6 climate projections to rank flood risk across India's arid Ramsar wetlands.

      Title: Flood risk in India's arid Ramsar wetlands: Integrating extreme rainfall, fuzzy risk assessment, and CMIP6 projections

      Authors: Dr. Shivukumar Rakkasagi, Kushal Jagdish Patil, Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal, and Dr. Shimrit Maman, PhD Maman Department of Civil Engineering, IIT Indore & Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Israel

      🔗 Read the paper: https://lnkd.in/dh5xjFf6


      Key Highlights:
      - First integrated flood-risk assessment of 17 arid Ramsar wetlands in India, combining extreme-value statistics, fuzzy-logic risk, and climate projections.

      - The climate driver varies by region: ENSO in Gujarat, IOD in southern India, AMO in the Indo-Gangetic Plain no one-size-fits-all model works.

      - Six wetlands rank "very high" flood risk, led by Ranganathittu, Chitrangudi, and Sarsai Nawar Jheel.

      - The twist: Khijadia has the highest rainfall extremes but only moderate risk, so vulnerability and exposure, not rainfall alone, decide true risk.

      - Under high emissions (SSP585), all 17 sites face 3.5–5.0 °C warming by 2100; Paris-aligned action cuts that by approx 2–3 °C.

      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Israel Space Agency, Elsevier, Department of Science & Technology, Government of India

      We are pleased to share a significant milestone from the Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore

      Our research group has successfully published three peer-reviewed studies focused on the detection, characterization, prediction, and societal implications of Aerosol Atmospheric Rivers (AARs) - an emerging and rapidly evolving area of atmospheric and environmental research. AARs are narrow corridors of extreme aerosol transport that can significantly influence air quality, climate, ecosystems, and human health across regional and continental scales.

      What makes this achievement particularly noteworthy is that Aerosol Atmospheric Rivers remain a relatively new scientific concept, with only six studies reported globally to date. Among these contributions, three have originated from our lab, reflecting our commitment to advancing the understanding of extreme aerosol transport processes and their environmental consequences.
      Our recent studies have focused on:
      * Global detection and climatology of Aerosol Atmospheric Rivers.
      * Deep learning-based frameworks for AAR prediction and forecasting.
      * Assessment of societal, environmental, and resilience implications associated with extreme aerosol transport events.

      These contributions provide a foundation for future research on aerosol transport dynamics, air pollution management, climate resilience, and early-warning systems for extreme aerosol events.

      We would like to especially acknowledge the outstanding contributions of Dr. Kuldeep Singh Rautela and Dr. Shivam Singh, whose dedication, innovation, and persistent efforts have been instrumental in advancing this research. Their work has significantly contributed to establishing the Water, Climate & Sustainability Lab as one of the leading contributors in the emerging field of Aerosol Atmospheric Rivers (AARs).

      Research Alert!
      As climate volatility increasingly defines the operating environment for business, this study in the Journal of Cleaner Production (Elsevier) remains a clear-eyed account of a question that has only grown more urgent: how should organizations distinguish the climate risks that demand action today from those that can be monitored over time?
      The work argues that extreme weather has moved beyond a facilities problem into the core of financial risk, and proposes a structured way to fuse climate-risk assessment with artificial intelligence using deep learning to forecast extreme-weather hazards far enough in advance to act on them.

      Title: Enhancing climate resilience in businesses: The role of artificial intelligence
      Authors: Dr. Shivam Singh and Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal Department of Civil Engineering, IIT Indore

      🔗 Read the paper: https://lnkd.in/d-Cr9ND9


      Key Highlights:
      - Every 1 °C rise in average temperature is estimated to cut global GDP by approx1.2%, making climate risk a core financial concern, not just an environmental one.
      - Proposes a vulnerability-and-risk framework built on Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability x Exposure, screening businesses into three tiers: act now, monitor, or no action required.
      - Maps climate impacts across 9 commercial sectors, energy, mining, food, transport, construction, water, manufacturing, insurance, and IT, and introduces "climate interpreters" to translate climate science into business decisions.
      - Frames a climate-resilient business ecosystem around four principles: robustness, redundancy, resourcefulness, and rapidity.
      - A deep-learning case study uses a Convolutional Autoencoder trained on ERA5/ECMWF data (2011–2018, 128,521 detected AR objects) to predict atmospheric rivers, achieving SSIM 0.74 and PSNR 64.4 dB, outperforming a comparable Conv-LSTM benchmark.

      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, DST - Centre for Policy Research, IIT Indore, Elsevier, Department of Science & Technology, Government of India

      New Research Alert!
      Wetlands store our water, shelter biodiversity, and buffer floods and droughts, but what happens when monsoons grow erratic and cities keep expanding into their catchments?
      Our latest study, published in Sustainable Development (Wiley), synthesises how climate change and human pressure are reshaping the inland wetlands of Central India, and why basin-scale, SDG-aligned management is now essential for water security.

      Title: Climate Change, Wetland Resilience, and the Sustainable Development Goals in Central India: Implications for Water Security and Adaptation Policy

      Authors: Amitoj raj, Dr. Kuldeep Singh Rautela, and Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal Department of Civil Engineering & Mehta Family School of Sustainability, IIT Indore

      Read the paper here: https://lnkd.in/dWVYshbg


      Key Highlights:
      - Reviewed 127 studies (from 2,159 screened) covering wetlands across the Narmada, Mahanadi, and Godavari basins.
      - Methane emissions reached 167 mg per square meter per hour at Dalpatsagar, while reservoir sedimentation has reduced storage capacity by 9 -13% (Tawa lost approx 212.6 MCM over 50 years).
      - Bhopal's built-up area increased from 8.82% to 25.79% (1990 -2020), placing pressure on the Bhoj Wetland, which supplies 40% of drinking water to 1.8 million residents.
      - Urban lakes showed emerging microplastic contamination of up to 12.3 items per liter, contributing to declining water quality.
      - Recommends basin-scale, climate-resilient wetland management aligned with SDGs 6, 13, and 15 through integrated planning, continuous monitoring, and nature-based solutions.

      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, DST - Centre for Policy Research, IIT Indore, Wiley, Department of Science & Technology, Government of India, Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore

      We are proud to announce the publication of our new research book:

      📘 "Environmental Monitoring with Integrated Earth Observation Data and Machine Learning"

      Authored by Dr. Srija Roy and Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal from the Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, and published by Springer Nature in the Studies in Computational Intelligence series (Vol. 1278, 2026).

      🔗 Access the book here: https://lnkd.in/dcR-TMYv


      🌍 The book demonstrates how Earth Observation and Machine Learning can be integrated to monitor land use, human pressures, water stress, and air quality at basin scale synthesized into a composite Environmental Monitoring Index (EMI) through a detailed case study of the Narmada River Basin, India. It offers researchers, policymakers, and practitioners a practical, evidence-based framework for data-driven environmental decision-making.

      Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal reposted this
      Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal • 3rd+ Chair Professor, Former Dean (2020-2025) 2mo •
      Pleased to share a major milestone from our research group at IIT Indore — we have been granted 02 Indian Patents in the domain of Wetland Science and Remote Sensing Technology! Congratulations to Dr. Vijay Jain and Utkarsh Yadav

      🔬 Patent 1: Method and System for Risk Assessment and Management for a Wetland

      This invention presents a data-driven framework integrating climate, hydrological, and environmental datasets to assess wetland risk in real time. It evaluates hazards from both climate change-induced precipitation extremes and anthropogenic pressures, computes vulnerability through Wetland Health and Exposure Scores, and generates automated conservation and mitigation reports — enabling informed decision-making for wetland restoration.

      🛰️ Patent 2: A System and Method for Monitoring Water Quality of a Wetland

      This invention introduces a satellite-based system using high-resolution imagery to monitor wetland water quality in near-real time. Key innovations include multi-spectral index computation (NDCI, NDMI, NDTI, NDWI), cloud masking, and historical gap-filling — enabling scalable monitoring of eutrophication and turbidity with a user-friendly reporting interface.

      These patents represent years of interdisciplinary work at the intersection of earth observation, environmental science, and climate resilience. We believe these technologies can play a meaningful role in India's wetland conservation mission — particularly for Ramsar Sites and ecologically sensitive water bodies.

      We are actively looking to collaborate with government agencies, environmental organisations, and research institutions. If you are working in wetland management, remote sensing, or climate adaptation — let's connect! 🤝

      MoEF&CC Indian Institute of Technology Indore Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore Wetlands International

      Highlighting Innovation: IIT Indore's Green Transformation Featured in Times of India!

      We are thrilled to see our campus water conservation project spotlighted by The Times of India.
      Under the guidance of Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal, our team integrated satellite-based monitoring (NDVI tracking) with smart engineering, such as check dams and rainwater harvesting, to fight peak summer dry spells.

      The Results (2021 to 2025):
      Thriving Greenery: Proven, steady rise in vegetation density and plant health.
      Water Security: Enhanced groundwater recharge and long-term soil moisture retention.
      Climate Resilience: Reduced soil erosion and a cooler local campus temperature.

      As our Director, Prof. Suhas Joshi, stated, this is a powerful validation of what happens when scientific insight is translated into purposeful action. Proud of the collective effort from our researchers and collaborators in driving real-world environmental impact!

      Read the full feature in TOI: https://lnkd.in/dFmSYv-a

      📖 This book bridges 𝗘𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗘𝗢) and 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗠𝗟) to address real-world environmental monitoring challenges spanning land degradation, water scarcity, urban expansion, and air quality. It covers EO data management and processing tools, ML algorithms for environmental analysis, and applied case studies. A comprehensive assessment of the 𝗡𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗮 𝗥𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗻 covers topography, climate variability, LULC dynamics, water stress under climate change projections, and a novel 𝗘𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝘅 developed using Machine Learning.

      📌 𝗔𝘃𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝘁: 🛒 Amazon: https://lnkd.in/dZAKqqaE

      🔗 Springer: https://lnkd.in/dvMb_nfu


      This work would not have been possible without the vision and mentorship of my supervisor, Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal. His ability to connect satellite signals, water systems, and actionable science shaped the very idea and architecture of this book. I am deeply grateful. I also feel incredibly fortunate to be part of the Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, a close circle of friends and colleagues that offered constant feedback, intellectual stimulation, and support at every stage of this book. To the entire cNarmada IIT Indore, thank you for the collaboration, shared purpose, and motivation that kept this work grounded and meaningful 🙏

      Sunil Chaturvedi • 3rd+ Hydrogeologist | Social Reformer | Water Conservation Expert | Author | Founder at Vibhavari 3mo •
      Is Indore becoming the next Bengaluru?

      With groundwater levels in Indore reportedly dropping to 560 feet and borewell restrictions making a comeback, the signs of urban water stress are hard to ignore. We are witnessing a familiar pattern: rapid urbanization is cutting off natural recharge paths just as our demand peaks.

      Bengaluru serves as a stark reminder of what happens when we prioritize extraction over recharge. We still have a window to act, but it requires a fundamental shift in how we manage our water.

      The path forward is clear:

      * Mandatory Recharge: Rainwater harvesting must be functional in every large building, not just on paper.
      * Restore Natural Assets: Our lakes and ponds are vital recharge zones that need immediate protection.
      * Circular Use: Treated water must be integrated into our urban systems for non-potable needs.
      * Proactive Planning: Water security needs to be the foundation of urban development, not a seasonal reaction to a crisis.

      The cities that thrive tomorrow will be those that secure their water today.

      For others, it will be an endless cycle of crisis management.

      The time for collective action is now.

      New Research Alert!

      Wetlands sustain biodiversity, regulate climate, and purify our water, but what happens when rainfall itself becomes unpredictable? Our latest study, published in Environmental Impact Assessment Review, uncovers how climate change is reshaping the hydrological future of 2,490 Ramsar wetlands worldwide, with arid regions emerging as surprising hotspots of vulnerability.

      Title: The future of global Ramsar wetlands under intensifying precipitation extremes: Arid regions as emerging hotspots

      Authors: Deepak Mishra, Nakka Naveen Kumar, Dr. Shekhar Singh, and Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore

      Read the paper here: https://lnkd.in/dj4xjVRG


      Key Highlights:
      Analysed 2,490 Ramsar wetlands across 172 countries using 13 CMIP6 models spanning 1951 to 2100.
      Arid wetlands grew by 14.5% and annual rainfall rose 9.3%, yet hydrological stress is rising sharply.
      Extreme rainfall frequency (RR95) climbed 16.36%, with intensity (SDII) up 9.5% in arid zones.
      Over 95% of temperate wetlands and 80% of arid wetlands now exceed extreme rainfall thresholds.
      A paradoxical risk emerges: more rainfall, but in shorter, fiercer bursts that fuel flash floods and disrupt fragile ecosystems.
      Findings call for climate-resilient wetland policies aligned with SDG 13 and SDG 14, including early warning systems and nature-based solutions.

      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, DST - Centre for Policy Research, IIT Indore,Ministry of Earth Sciences, Ministry of Science and Technology, Elsevier, Department of Science & Technology, Government of India

      New Research Alert!
      We can monitor cyclones in real time and forecast floods in advance. Why not landfills? That's the question behind our latest study in Scientific Reports (Springer Nature) and the answer is a satellite-based framework that measures how much waste is piling up across India, without sending a single surveyor to the ground.

      Title: High-Resolution Landfill Characterization Using SAR Remote Sensing and Cloud-Based Processing

      Authors: Shashank Agrawal, Dr. Shivukumar Rakkasagi & Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal Indian Institute of Technology, Indore

      Read the full open-access paper here: https://lnkd.in/df_2nuh5


      What's new this time:
      A Python plus SNAP plus Google Earth Engine pipeline that turns free Sentinel-1 SAR data into 10 m Digital Elevation Models, capturing waste pile height and volume from space

      Applied to 80 landfill sites across India, the first nationwide SAR-based assessment of landfill volume using a single replicable method

      An adaptive volume algorithm that handles both small dumpsites and mega landfills, with mode filtering for sparse pixels and direct statistics for dense ones

      Ground-truthed at Gondiya and Ujjain using DGPS, total station, and drone surveys, with field validation error as low as 0.12 to 0.80% at the Ujjain site

      Key numbers from the study:
      Chennai Dumping Ground: 33.7 million cubic metres of waste
      Mumbai's Deonar: 25.8 million cubic metres
      Smaller sites (under 60,000 sq m) stay below 5 m in height
      Legacy sites exceed 60,000 sq m and reach up to 39 m of accumulated waste

      The gap this closes. We already track deforestation, floods, and crop health from space. Landfills have been the missing piece, still mapped with measuring tapes and clipboards. This study brings them into the same observational system, making every dumping ground in the country measurable, comparable, and trackable over time, supporting capacity planning, environmental assessment, and data-driven waste policy.

      Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, DST - Centre for Policy Research, IIT Indore, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs,
      Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate Change, Government of India
      Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), National Mission For Clean Ganga
      NITI Aayog, Indore Municipal Corporation

      New research Alert!

      The air we breathe is the most invisible infrastructure of all. Air pollution causes 4.2 million premature deaths each year, and India is home to 22 of the world's 30 most polluted cities. Yet most urban airsheds still lack a way to forecast the next severe pollution episode, or to explain why it happens.
      What if we could rebuild four decades of air quality history, identify the weather conditions that trigger extreme PM₂.₅ events, and forecast them with explainable AI in one framework any city can adopt?
      That's the question behind our study in Physics and Chemistry of the Earth (Elsevier).

      Title: AI-driven air quality mapping and forecasting for extreme PM₂.₅ events
      Authors: Dr. Kuldeep Singh Rautela, Mayank upadhyay, Prof. Manish Kumar Goyal, Sitaram Taigor
      Indian Institute of Technology, Indore | Urban Administration and Development, Bhopal

      Read the full paper here: https://lnkd.in/gEav3e_y


      What's new this time:
      44 years of PM₂.₅ reconstructed (1980 to 2023) over the Indore urban airshed by fusing MERRA-2 reanalysis with IMD and CPCB/MPPCB observations

      Eight ML/DL models combined into a bias-corrected ensemble reaching R² of 0.80 to 0.92 across train, validation, and test phases

      SHAP-based explainable AI showing that sustained thermal stagnation and ventilation efficiency, not instantaneous weather, drive extreme pollution

      Regulatory exceedances climbing at +2.06 days per year, with winter Sen's slopes 3 to 6 times higher than other seasons and no measurable improvement after the National Clean Air Programme

      GEV modelling showing that 20 to 50 year PM₂.₅ events now reach 170 to 220 μg/m³, meaning return intervals for hazardous concentrations are shrinking fast

      The bigger idea? Stop treating air pollution as a chronic background condition and start treating it as an extreme event, one that can be forecast, attributed, and acted on with the same urgency we give floods and cyclones.



      Water Climate and Sustainability Lab, IIT Indore, DST - Centre for Policy Research, IIT Indore, Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate Change, Government of India, Ministry of Earth Sciences, Ministry of Science and Technology, NITI Aayog
